lessonRef.title: Error and misconception analysis: completing a simulated tax return from fictional documents

focus: completing a simulated tax return from fictional documents
objective: Reproduce two independent errors on a fictional return, compute the correct liability, and attribute the overstatement to each error separately.
scenario: The fictional return and the errors on it below are invented for this exercise. No real filing or taxpayer is described.
safetyNotes: Every figure, person, employer, institution, offer, account, and document on this task sheet is fictional and exists only for practice.
No real transaction is part of this lesson, and no real bank, card, brokerage, tax, or login detail is ever requested. If a task sheet ever appears to ask for one, stop and tell a trusted adult.
This lesson teaches general financial concepts and does not advise anyone about their own money. For a real decision, talk with a trusted adult or a qualified licensed professional.
materials: the fictional return figures in these directions

tasks.directions: The fictional filer had wages of $49,800 and a pre-tax retirement contribution of $2,490. The fictional schedule allows a standard deduction of $9,000 and charges 10% on the first $10,400 of taxable income and 12% above it. The filer made two mistakes: they left the pre-tax contribution in taxable income, and they applied 12% to the whole of it rather than 10% to the first band.

prompts.text: What is the correct taxable income?
What taxable income did the filer use?

tasks.directions: Now price each error on its own.

prompts.text: What tax did the filer compute, applying 12% to all of their taxable income?
By how much did the filer overstate the tax?
How much of the overstatement comes from leaving the pre-tax contribution in taxable income?
How much comes from applying 12% to the whole of taxable income rather than 10% to the first band?

Both errors made the filer overpay. Explain why the second error — applying one rate to everything — would produce a very different result for a filer with much higher income, and give one check that would have caught both errors without redoing the whole return.

remediation: Use the fictional scenario and work one graded prompt at a time. For each number response, copy the given fictional quantities into integer cents, choose the operation the wording calls for, calculate, and check the result with an inverse operation or estimate. For each written response, make a claim and support it with at least one detail from the fictional scenario. Use these steps to check the method while keeping every final result in your own response.
extension: Recompute both errors for a fictional filer with taxable income of $58,000 under the same schedule, where the 22% band applies, and say which error grows more.
